messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 45
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Combat Pilot
- Trauma Type: Terrorism
- Pcl5: 56

She is 45, a combat pilot with two decades in uniform, and she still thinks of the day of the attack in fragments of sound before anything else: the clipped voices in her headset, the sudden break in routine, the flat certainty in the operations officer’s face when the first reports come through. She is on base that morning, preparing for a training sortie, moving through familiar checks with the calm precision that has shaped most of her adult life. Then the alarms begin. At first there is confusion—rumor, partial information, people running in different directions while trying to stay disciplined. Then there is smoke visible beyond the perimeter, dark and rising in a way that does not belong to training.

The attack is later described as terrorism, coordinated and deliberate. What she remembers is how quickly the ordinary world disappears. She remembers the force of the secondary blast, the way it seems to punch the air from her lungs even at a distance. She remembers seeing one of the hangars burning and a medic kneeling beside someone she recognizes by boots and posture before she can recognize his face. She is ordered into the air with others, not to engage at first but to secure the surrounding zone, and she does what she has always done under pressure: narrows, focuses, performs. She flies the aircraft flawlessly. It is only after landing, when she takes off her helmet, that her hands begin to shake.

In the days afterward, she does not have the luxury of falling apart. There are investigations, briefings, memorials, and revised security procedures. She tells herself that staying busy is the same as coping. People around her praise her professionalism. She accepts it because she does not know what else to do. At night, though, she lies awake in the dark of her quarters with her body still braced for impact. If she sleeps, she wakes with her heart racing, hearing the blast again or smelling jet fuel mixed with smoke. She starts leaving the television off because footage of attacks, sirens, or even crowded city scenes can suddenly flood her with the same electric panic.

Before the attack, flying is the place where she feels most fully herself—competent, clear, contained. Afterward, the cockpit becomes complicated. She still performs well, but now every unexpected radio transmission jolts through her. During preflight, she finds herself scanning the tarmac, the fencing, the rooftops beyond the base, never quite satisfied that she has checked enough. She tells no one how often she mentally rehearses escape routes from briefing rooms, cafeterias, hotels on temporary assignment. In civilian airports she cannot relax at all. She studies unattended bags, watches people’s hands, notices who is wearing bulky jackets in warm weather. She chooses seats near exits and keeps her back to walls.

She has always been private, but after the attack she becomes harder to reach. She is single, and where she once maintained a small but meaningful circle of friends from her squadron, she now turns down invitations with excuses that sound reasonable even to her. She says she is tired, has paperwork, needs sleep before an early flight. The truth is that restaurants feel exposed, celebrations feel wrong, and casual laughter can make her strangely angry. She cannot explain why other people’s ease feels like an insult. More than once she snaps at colleagues for minor breaches in protocol, then goes home ashamed and unable to stop replaying the exchange.

There are moments that disturb her most because they seem so unlike her. A fuel truck backfiring on base sends her ducking instinctively behind a vehicle before she can think. A crowded holiday market in town leaves her drenched in sweat, searching for threats and exits while her chest tightens so badly she has to leave without buying anything. On anniversaries of the attack, her body seems to know the date before her mind does. She becomes irritable, restless, and unable to concentrate. She drinks more than she used to on those nights, not enough to lose control, she insists, just enough to blunt the edges and make sleep possible.

She carries guilt that does not yield to logic. She knows, factually, that she did what was required of her. She knows she could not have prevented the deaths that day. Still, she thinks of the people who did not make it and feels she has no right to complain because she survived, flew, functioned. When younger pilots come to her for guidance, she is respected and even admired, but she often feels like she is impersonating the officer they believe her to be.

Now, years later, she remains highly capable, sharply intelligent, and outwardly composed. Most people see discipline and steadiness. They do not see that she sleeps lightly with her phone beside her bed, or that she startles at footsteps in the hallway, or that she avoids certain parts of the base because the angle of a building can bring the whole morning rushing back. She says the attack is never entirely in the past. It lives in her body first—in the tension of her shoulders, the constant scan of her eyes, the way her breath catches when the world becomes unpredictable. She keeps going, because that is what she has always done, but the cost of that endurance is with her every day.
